title: The Battle Over Mail-in Voting May Disrupt the 2026 Midterm Elections | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: The Supreme Court's procedural (not substantive) ruling lifting an injunction on Trump's USPS mail-ballot restrictions leaves a 'Purcell principle' trap where courts could later refuse to rule because it is too close to the election, threatening to disrupt 2026 midterm mail voting even as early voting begins in most states by late October.

themes.theme: The Purcell principle trap on mail-in voting

insights.claim: The Supreme Court's unsigned opinion lifting the injunction against USPS mail-ballot restrictions turned on procedural standing grounds (the 23 states plus DC sued before suffering concrete harm), not on the constitutionality of Trump's directive — leaving the substantive question of whether the president can use the Postal Service to regulate state-run elections still unresolved.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Because the ruling was procedural, the underlying constitutional fight over federal control of mail voting remains live and could resurface with less runway before the election.
insights.quote: The Court's disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell.

insights.claim: Legal experts fear the Supreme Court could invoke the 'Purcell principle' — that federal courts should not change election rules close to an election — to let the USPS Final Rule take effect by default, even though the Court has itself been inconsistent in applying Purcell this term in Texas, Louisiana, and Alabama.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: This creates a legal 'Catch-22': having ruled in August it was too early to decide the constitutional question, the Court could rule in September/October it is now too late — a scenario that would let contested USPS rules stand without ever being substantively reviewed.
insights.quote: to hide behind it to allow the USPS Final Rule to go into effect would be as indefensible and anti-democratic a ruling as the Court has handed down in a very long time

insights.claim: The USPS Final Rule requires states to submit voter lists through a not-yet-built Federal Ballot Mail Portal and to print ballot materials meeting new design standards, with noncompliant ballots not mailed or processed — a federal Postal Service mandate on state election administration operationalized through mail-delivery mechanics rather than legislation.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: The Portal not yet existing is a hard operational bottleneck — states have limited time to comply, and any last-minute rollout failure would directly disrupt ballot mailing.
insights.locator: Middle paragraphs on the Final Rule

insights.claim: The Postal Service has a mixed record handling mail ballots and no election-management expertise; Michigan rejected 10,000 primary ballots last month for arriving late, twice the 2024 rate, and a federal whistleblower alleges the Postal Service plans to randomly validate ballots such that if one chosen ballot in a batch fails to match the voter register, the entire batch is rejected.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: The batch-rejection validation method, if implemented, could disenfranchise valid voters en masse due to a single mismatched ballot in their batch — a concrete operational risk ahead of a nationally consequential midterm.
insights.locator: Body paragraph on Postal Service record

insights.claim: Four states begin voting in September, another 17 begin early voting by October 14, and by October 29 voters in all but three states (Alabama, New Hampshire, Mississippi) will have the opportunity to cast ballots — meaning many votes will be cast well before Election Day, reducing the potential impact of late-breaking campaign events.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Campaign strategists and forecasters should weight pre-October developments more heavily than traditional 'October surprise' dynamics, since a large share of the electorate votes before then.

insights.claim: Nearly one in three Americans voted by mail in 2024, though that share may not hold in a lower-turnout midterm; more Democrats than Republicans vote by mail, but restrictions could disproportionately burden older, rural voters — who lean Republican — given their relative difficulty reaching polling places or drop-off boxes.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Because restrictions could cut both ways politically (hurting Democrat-leaning mail voters but also Republican-leaning rural/older voters), the net partisan effect of the USPS rule is genuinely uncertain — a key unknown for anyone modeling midterm outcomes.

insights.claim: Trump's net approval rating stands at -19.1 points (38.6% approve, 57.7% disapprove) as of the article date, close to his 2026 low of -20.6 points, while Republicans' consumer sentiment fell 9.5 points from July to August per the University of Michigan survey — one of the biggest monthly drops in the survey's history and worse than the 8% overall decline.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
entities: University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey
insights.so_what: A sharp, Republican-specific consumer sentiment drop alongside near-record-low presidential approval suggests economic headwinds (noted alongside still-elevated gas prices around $4.09/gallon) are eroding Trump's own base ahead of the midterms.

insights.claim: Larry Sabato's Crystal Ball rates 22 House seats as toss-ups (17 currently/previously Republican-held, 5 Democratic), with the two newest additions moving from 'leans Republican'; on the Senate side, five seats are toss-ups (Alaska, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and newly added Texas), giving both parties a plausible path to Senate control.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: Texas newly appearing as a Senate toss-up is a notable shift worth tracking, since it would represent a meaningful expansion of competitive terrain beyond traditional swing states.

insights.claim: Two more House Democratic incumbents lost primaries in August, bringing the cycle total to seven — the most primary losses for House Democrats since 2012 — but the author notes 2012's tough primary cycle preceded Democrats gaining eight House seats that November, meaning primary losses are not necessarily a dark omen for the general election.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: This historical parallel argues against over-reading incumbent primary losses as a negative signal for November — a useful corrective for anyone extrapolating primary results into general-election forecasts.

insights.claim: As of the article date, 13 senators and 72 representatives (16 percent of all congressional seats) have declined to run for reelection, cannot run, or lost their primary — guaranteeing at least 85 new faces in the next Congress, a number likely to grow before and on Election Day.
insights.speaker: James M. Lindsay
insights.so_what: A guaranteed minimum 16% turnover rate signals a substantial reshaping of Congress's composition regardless of which party wins, relevant for anyone modeling post-2026 legislative dynamics.
